cards.info: What is the definition of random assignment in an experiment?
cards.backInfo: Using chance to assign participants to treatment groups to ensure groups are similar at the start.

cards.info: What is the primary purpose of using random assignment?
cards.backInfo: To reduce the impact of confounding variables by balancing them across treatment groups.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: What role does a control group play in an experimental study?
cards.backInfo: It consists of participants who receive no active treatment, serving as a baseline for comparison.

cards.info: What is a placebo in the context of a control group?
cards.backInfo: A neutral or 'sham' treatment used to account for the psychological effect of receiving treatment.

cards.info: What does 'double-blind' mean in an experimental design?
cards.backInfo: Neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the active treatment.

cards.info: Which design element most directly reduces bias from participant expectations?
cards.backInfo: Blinding is the most direct method to reduce bias resulting from participant or researcher expectations.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: What is expectation bias in a study?
cards.backInfo: When a participant's knowledge of their treatment status influences their reported symptoms or behavior.

cards.info: How is replication performed in an experimental study?
cards.backInfo: By repeating the study with different participants or using a larger sample size to verify consistency.

cards.info: What is the benefit of increasing a study's sample size?
cards.backInfo: It improves the precision of results and reduces the impact of random sampling error.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: Does a control group alone prevent expectation bias?
cards.backInfo: No; blinding is required to stop the participant from knowing their group assignment and biasing data.

cards.info: How does random assignment differ from self-selection in group formation?
cards.backInfo: Random assignment uses chance to ensure groups are similar, whereas self-selection allows participant choice to introduce bias.

cards.info: Which design element balances unknown outside factors across treatment groups?
cards.backInfo: Random assignment balances confounding variables so that groups are as similar as possible at the start.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: Why is a baseline comparison necessary in an experiment?
cards.backInfo: A control group provides a baseline to separate the treatment's effect from natural changes.

cards.info: What is the purpose of giving a 'sham' treatment to a control group?
cards.backInfo: A placebo accounts for the psychological effect of receiving treatment rather than the treatment's actual chemical effect.

cards.info: What is the difference between single-blind and double-blind studies?
cards.backInfo: Single-blind hides treatment status from participants; double-blind hides it from both participants and researchers.

cards.info: Which tool most directly prevents a researcher from influencing a study's results?
cards.backInfo: Double-blinding prevents researcher influence by keeping them unaware of which participants receive the active treatment.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: How does knowing one's treatment status threaten a study's validity?
cards.backInfo: It causes expectation bias, where the participant's knowledge changes their reported behavior or symptoms.

cards.info: What procedure ensures that a study's results were not a one-time fluke?
cards.backInfo: Replication, which involves repeating the study or using a large sample size to ensure consistency.

cards.info: How does replication affect the impact of sampling error?
cards.backInfo: Replication reduces the impact of random sampling error and increases the precision of the findings.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart showing the mapping of design elements to the biases they mitigate: Randomization to Confounding, Blinding to Expectation, and Replication to Low Precision.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f459edfa-ff2c-4be0-a80c-e4379ec2f06d-1786506161766-684.webp)

cards.info: Why is a control group insufficient to stop expectation bias?
cards.backInfo: Without blinding, participants still know their group assignment, which allows their expectations to influence the data.
